abstract:
AI-generated videos often depict people within detailed scenes while leaving their small facial regions poorly resolved. Visual super-resolution can sharpen these regions without resolving whether the recovered lips and teeth agree with the spoken audio. We present an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that addresses this ambiguity within a reference-guided video flow model. Source–noise mixing initializes reconstruction from a partially preserved observation, and structured reference injection separates appearance anchors from continuous motion context. Training combines restoration of degraded images and videos with correction of degraded dubbed sources under target audio. Appearance and synchronization supervision allow the model to recover facial detail and support visual dubbing when the audio is replaced. On talking-head restoration benchmarks, our method achieves the best paired perceptual similarity and synchronization scores among the compared restoration methods. Component comparisons examine audio conditioning, the reconstruction formulation, and reference injection. Native AIGC examples further illustrate the recovery of lip contours, dental structure, and surrounding facial texture in scene-level footage.

Project page: https://taoliveaigc.github.io/TaoMate-FVSR/

sections.body: The paper argues that a high-resolution frame does not guarantee a high-resolution face. In medium and full-body shots, lips, teeth, and the oral cavity can stay blurred. The authors propose an audio-guided restoration framework built on a reference-guided video flow model. Training combines restoration of degraded images and videos with correction of degraded dubbed sources paired with target audio. The three listed contributions are: audio-guided restoration that supports both original-audio restoration and replacement-audio dubbing; a source–noise reconstruction formulation trained with visual-restoration and cross-articulation objectives; and structured reference injection that places sparse references and continuous motion history in separate temporal slots.
sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.headline: Restoring small AIGC faces requires lip and teeth detail that agrees with the spoken audio, not only sharper pixels.

sections.body: Facial and video restoration includes GAN-prior methods such as GFP-GAN and GPEN, diffusion-based image restoration such as StableSR and SUPIR, and recurrent video propagation such as BasicVSR++. Generative video restoration includes Upscale-A-Video, SeedVR2, FlashVSR, and SparkVSR. The authors state that they couple facial-detail recovery with target-audio control and cross-articulation supervision. Visual dubbing work includes Wav2Lip, VideoReTalking, LatentSync, and X-Dub. Audio-assisted restoration work includes talking-face upsampling and MDVD-Net. The authors state that they focus on restoration when the observed mouth is unreliable or incompatible with replacement audio.
sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.headline: Related work spans facial and video restoration, generative restoration, visual dubbing, and audio-assisted restoration; the authors focus on unreliable mouths.

sections.body: The model reconstructs a facial video in a latent flow model from a low-quality video, target audio, and appearance references. Source–noise mixing sets the starting point: the source latent is mixed with Gaussian noise at strength $\rho\in[0.80,0.95]$, so the output need not copy unreliable mouth detail. Sparse clean reference frames occupy one temporal slot as appearance anchors, while four adjacent frames form a separate motion-context slot. Training has two stages. Stage one restores degraded images and videos. Stage two performs audio-guided lip correction on degraded dubbed sources, with a frozen SyncNet supplying synchronization supervision. At inference, the reference is the ground-truth first frame or a GPT-Image-enhanced version of it.
sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.headline: The method mixes source latents with noise to start flow reconstruction and injects sparse references and history into separate temporal slots.

sections.body: The benchmark uses 150 videos from MEAD, HDTF, TalkVid, and an internal dataset. Ours reaches LPIPS 0.0793 and DISTS 0.0858, against 0.1380 and 0.1421 for InstantRestore. Its Sync-C and Sync-D are 7.413 and 7.561, compared with 6.545 and 8.170 for SparkVSR. SparkVSR has the highest PSNR at 30.62 and SSIM at 0.8863, which exceed Ours by 1.95 dB and 0.0027. The enhanced-reference row, Ours+, has the highest no-reference quality scores but lower PSNR at 23.52. In ablations, removing audio gives Sync-C and Sync-D of 4.283 and 10.524, against 7.621 and 7.560 for Ours. The adapted X-Dub variant and DirectMotion both have higher LPIPS and worse synchronization than Ours.
sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.headline: On the 150-video benchmark, Ours has the lowest paired perceptual error, while SparkVSR leads pixel-level fidelity.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the reported results: lower paired perceptual error and better synchronization than the evaluated restoration baselines, replacement-audio dubbing without a separate mouth-editing model, and recovery of facial regions within larger scenes. The authors state that reconstructed facial detail is a generative estimate, not evidence of true appearance. They also state that audio-driven editing can facilitate impersonation. Accordingly, applications should obtain appropriate permission and clearly disclose edited content.
sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors state that reconstructed facial detail is a generative estimate, not evidence of true appearance, and raise impersonation risk.
